_doc: NPC_AI_SPEC §10's build-order item 7 (Combat + companion) — every tunable
the combat-category actions read. §12's rule applies: nothing in
src/ai/actions/takeCover.ts or engageThreat.ts hardcodes a number that
belongs here.
Kept separate from perception.json rather than folded into it: phase 6
owns what an agent KNOWS, this file owns what it DOES about it, and the
two are tuned against different things (a sight range against the bow's
reach, a cover standoff against a building's real footprint). The one
genuine coupling — cover.minThreat against perception.json's
hearing.confidence — is spelled out below rather than left for a future
tuner to rediscover the hard way.
Reference points these were chosen against, same convention
perception.json's own _doc uses:
MELEE_RANGE 1.8         components/world/Defenders.tsx
melee attackCd 1.1s     components/world/Defenders.tsx
ENGAGE_RADIUS 22        Defenders.tsx — a SWORN defender's watch
RUN_SPEED 1.6 m/s       ai/core/Locomotion.ts (flee pace)
figure height 1.7       RiggedFigure height={1.7}, every minifig
STOP_DISTANCE 0.6       ai/actions/flee.ts — the existing arrival line
vision.range 16         ai/config/perception.json
hearing.confidence .35  ai/config/perception.json — a heard belief's cap
threat.closeDistance 4  ai/config/perception.json
threat.falloffDist 16   ai/config/perception.json
take_cover — an unarmed villager's real answer to a hostile they can
actually perceive. Distinct from flee_to_safety, which gates on the
global `raid` flag and runs to one fixed point: this one answers a
SPECIFIC believed hostile and puts a real standing structure between
itself and that hostile's last known position.
minThreat 0.4 is the load-bearing number and it is set deliberately
ABOVE perception.json's hearing.confidence (0.35), which is the ceiling a
heard-but-unseen belief can ever reach. That is what makes the alarm
below provably loop-free: hearing a neighbour's shout alone can never
push a villager over this line, so it can never make them shout in turn.
Against the §6.3 threat curve (full confidence x proximity, flat inside
closeDistance 4 and falling to nothing at falloffDistance 16) it works
out to 'a hostile I can SEE, inside about 9.6 m' — roughly the distance
at which a farmer would actually drop the hoe.
minThreat is an ENTRY threshold only, and that distinction was learned
the hard way: with it also acting as the exit test, take_cover never once
reached the cover it picked. Running away turns the villager's back on the
raider (yaw follows travel, and the 114.6-degree vision cone with it), so
the belief stops being refreshed and decays at 0.25/s while proximity
falls at the same time — threat is the product of the two, so it dropped
back under 0.4 within ~3s, which is shorter than most cover runs. The
action gated out mid-flight and left the villager standing in the open,
and around the boundary it alternated with idle_fidget twice in under two
seconds, re-picking a different destination each time. Two numbers fix
that, and both describe the same idea — a decision, once taken, is worth
seeing through:
commitSec 12   while still travelling, the action holds regardless of
what threat has since done. 12s is a backstop, not the
expected duration: at RUN_SPEED 1.6 it covers a ~19m run,
and a blocked path ends the travel phase early on its own
(bb.movement goes 'blocked', which counts as arrival).
A villager does not stop halfway to the barn because they
can no longer picture exactly where the raider was.
commitThreat   what the gate READS during that window — a flat number,
0.8            not the live threat, because it is answering 'am I still
running this' rather than 'how bad is it'. Its value is
pinned by one requirement: flee_to_safety must still be
able to take over at ANY point of the run, not only
inside minDuration. flee scores a flat 4.0 (one bool
consideration, survival weight) and the reasoner's
momentum x switch threshold means a challenger has to
clear score x 1.25 x 1.15. At 0.8 the curve gives 0.667,
scoreAction's two-consideration product gives 0.778, so
take_cover scores 2.33 and the bar for replacing it is
3.35 — under flee's 4.0, and far over the 1.4 the best
work action can reach. So 'during a raid flee still wins,
and nothing else interrupts a cover run' is arithmetic
here, not a hope. Saturating at 1.0 instead would put the
bar at 4.31 and quietly make a fleeing villager stay put.
sustainThreat  once STOOD DOWN behind the piece, threat only has to stay
0.15           above this to keep watching — classic hysteresis, entry
at 0.4, release at 0.15. From a lost sighting that is
ln(1/0.15)/0.25 = ~7.6s of watching before ordinary life
resumes, and re-entry then needs a genuine new 0.4-grade
scare rather than the same fading one wobbling over the
line. Still below hearing's 0.35 ceiling, so nothing about
the loop-freedom argument above changes.
minPieceHeight 1.6 is just under a minifig's own 1.7: a piece shorter
than the person hiding behind it is not cover, and this is read from the
buildable's real authored size (data/buildables.ts heightOf) rather than
from a hand-listed set of 'cover-ish' building types, which would rot the
first time a new wall piece shipped.
standoff 1.2 is measured from the piece's real FOOTPRINT edge (sizeFor,
projected onto the retreat direction), not from its centre — a 8m castle
wall and a 2m barrel need the same 'tucked in behind it' result from one
number. minRetreatGain 2 is the honesty check: a cover point must put at
least this much more distance between the villager and the threat than
they have now, or running to it is running TOWARD the raider.
standoffProbe/standoffStep exist because `sizeFor` and the nav grid do
NOT agree about how big a building is, and a single fixed offset silently
loses that argument. game/navgrid.ts inflates every collision box by
AGENT_RADIUS 0.55 and then stamps whole 1.0m cells, and a piece's
collision boxes are not always its authored display size — so blocked
ground can reach ~1.5m past the edge sizeFor reports, and further for a
piece whose collision volume is the larger of the two. Measured west of a
piece at x=-10: market_stall (half-width 1.3) first walkable 1.2m past
its edge, tower (2.0) 1.5m, storehouse (1.5) 2.0m. At a flat standoff of
1.2 the storehouse's stand point failed isWalkable, the candidate was
silently discarded, and the villager ran 8m into the open instead — 'get
behind that building' working or not working depending on how the
geometry happened to round. So the stand point is now PROBED outward
along the same retreat ray in standoffStep 0.5 increments until it lands
on walkable ground, up to standoffProbe 2.8m past the ideal (4.0m past
the footprint edge). Outward along that ray only: every probe position
still has the piece between the villager and the threat, and moving
further out only increases the minRetreatGain the candidate has to clear.
retreatDistance 8 is the no-cover fallback — ~5 s at RUN_SPEED 1.6, far
enough to matter, short enough that the villager stays in the settlement
instead of sprinting into the treeline. repathDistance 4 is how far the
believed threat position has to move before the cover choice is redone;
below that, re-picking every tick would make a villager dither in the
open, which is the one thing this action exists to stop.
A villager who breaks for cover shouts about it, and the shout is a real
§6.2 world sound (perception/sounds.ts) carrying the SIGHTED hostile's
own belief id — so a neighbour who hears it gains a low-confidence belief
about that same raider, at a fuzzed position, exactly as if they had
heard the fight themselves. That is the first thing in this project to
emit into the hearing sensor from the AI side rather than from
game/combat.ts, and it is what makes one villager's panic spread as
information instead of as a hardcoded broadcast.
It is emitted ONLY for a belief with isVisibleNow — i.e. something this
villager can actually see. A sound-derived belief is never visible (the
vision sensor is the only writer of that flag), so a shout can never
cause a shout, whatever the numbers do. Belt and braces on top of
cover.minThreat's own margin above hearing.confidence.
loudness 0.7 x hearing.radiusPerLoudness 24 = ~17 m of earshot, which is
about vision.range (16): a shout carries roughly as far as you can see,
so the villager who hears it is plausibly one who could have seen it.
cooldownSec 25 throttles the player-facing notice per HOSTILE, not per
villager — the same 'call each one out once' shape scoutReported
(game/defenders.ts) already uses for a scouting defender.
engage_threat — closing on a believed hostile and striking it. Offered
to the `guard` archetype only (config/archetypes.json), and gated on the
agent actually being ARMED: the damage comes from the same
defenderStrike() formula Defenders.tsx uses, and an unarmed farmer is not
quietly given a defender's swing. See engageThreat.ts's own header for
which population can and cannot reach this today.
reach 1.8 IS Defenders.tsx's MELEE_RANGE and swingSeconds 1.1 IS its
melee attackCd — same numbers, deliberately, because this is the same
swing by the same people with the same weapons. approachStop 1.4 is
inside reach so the walk finishes with the target comfortably in range
rather than exactly on the boundary, where a mob's own step would break
contact every other frame.
loseTargetSec is how long the activity keeps working a belief it can no
longer confirm before giving up — a raider who ducked behind the barn is
worth two seconds of searching the spot he was last seen at; a belief
that is simply decaying out is not worth standing over.
Wave 21 — engage_threat_villager: an ORDINARY (non-defender)
villager's own, much weaker version of `engage` above. A distinct
block on purpose, matching the distinct action file/id (see
ai/actions/engageThreatVillager.ts's own header) — nothing here is
allowed to silently drift the defender-tuned block above.
reach/approachStop mirror `engage`'s own geometry (same 1.8m contact
range, same 1.4m approach stop) — it is the same physical swing by
the same kind of person, just weaker (see game/villagerCombat.ts's
flat, unleveled damage constant). swingSeconds 1.3 sits between a
trained defender's practiced 1.1s and a skeleton's own 1.6s pace:
swings, but slower than someone trained.
closeRange 3.5 is engage.reach + engage.approachStop (1.8 + 1.4 =
3.2) plus a small margin — 'already near the threat when it
appears', not 'anywhere on the perceived map', so a whole roster
does not converge on one distant raider the instant it is noticed.
courageThreshold 6 reads data/attributes.ts's existing 1-10 courage
roll, with 5 as the baseline `defenderStrike()` already treats as
'no bonus' — 'above-average courage' is a real, non-arbitrary
cutoff, not an invented number.
capableTierMax 1 is this wave's own DPS/TTK simulation result: past
difficulty tier 1, `raidStrength()` (game/difficulty.ts) scales the
very skeletons a villager would fight faster than a villager's own
flat, unleveled stats can keep up with — a villager has no
gainDefenderXp-style growth the way a defender does.
Wave 25 — assist_leader (ai/actions/assistLeader.ts): Tam, the
companion squire's own combat rhythm. Same shape as `engage` above
(EngageConfig — reach/approachStop/swingSeconds/loseTargetSec, no new
interface needed), reach/approachStop identical to both `engage` and
`engageVillager` (same 1.8m contact range, same 1.4m approach stop —
it is the same physical swing by the same kind of person, just a
different strength). swingSeconds 1.2 is the exact numeric midpoint
between a villager's own 1.3s and a trained defender's 1.1s — see
game/companion.ts's own header for the full HP/damage/DPS table this
sits inside.
No closeRange/courageThreshold/capableTierMax fields (unlike
`engageVillager`): those three exist specifically to stop a whole
ROSTER of flat, unleveled villagers from mass-dogpiling into fights
their stats can't scale with as raidStrength() climbs. There is
exactly one companion, ever (falcon.ts's own 'one always-on
companion, not a fleet' precedent) — that risk cannot occur here, so
assist_leader's own gate is simply `agent.archetype === 'companion'`,
argued in full in that file's header.
leashDistance 20 (verification fix, post-ship) — Defenders.tsx's own
`ENGAGE_RADIUS` (how far a patrolling defender will spot a hostile in
the first place) is 20m from a fixed post; this reuses that same real
reference point but measures from the PLAYER instead, since a
companion's 'post' is wherever the player currently is. Past it,
assist_leader gives up on a target it cannot otherwise stop chasing
(see assistLeader.ts's own header) and hands back to follow_leader.
